There are other terminals storing transportation fuels throughout New England that could present an opportunity to accommodate SAF and Jet A storage and blending. The following terminal operators expressed a willingness to consider receipt, storage, and blending of locally produced SAF at their terminals: Buckeye Partners, Global Partners, Inland Fuel Terminals, Shell, Sprague Energy, and Sunoco Logistics. Several terminal companies mentioned that they would be more likely to recommend their terminals that currently store kerosene due to the similar properties with Jet A. Tank and capacity data for New England terminals not currently storing jet fuel are provided in Appendix C. Nearly all terminals lease tanks and associated equipment to third parties for storage and blending activities. Any terminal storing and blending SAF would require a capital investment to accommodate these activities. It is common to incorporate these investment costs into the lease agreement, or there is the option for the entity leasing the tanks to pay the capital investment upfront. Most tanks at terminals are in use, and available tanks could be cleaned and repurposed for SAF. Not all tanks are suitable for jet fuel storage, as a fixed roof is required, and not all distillate tanks are equipped with this roof type. It is preferred to use existing tanks due to lower costs; however, there is potential to build new tanks with the awareness that the permitting process could take years. A SAF facility would work directly with fuel terminals or through a fuel marketer to identify available tank capacity at preferred terminals. The results are intended to help New England states prepare for future SAF availability and to highlight opportunities for regional production. This report evaluated the potential for local production due to the potential positive economic impacts of converting nearby waste and other feedstocks into SAF for use at New England airports. The resource assessment found that MSW and food waste are the most abundant resources within 50- and 100-mile radii, reflecting the airports’ locations in densely populated urban areas. Woody biomass was highest near PWM given Maine’s well established wood products industry. While the focus of this study was SAF, the resource assessment is useful for production of other biofuels, biochemicals, and bioenergy.
